It was not "killed;" it was only superseded and therefore should retain the position it held last night. The bill was not in committee of the whole. Standing order 15, subsection 4 reads:
After a private or public bill has been considered on Tuesday or Friday evening and debate thereon has been adjourned or interrupted at nine o'clock, it shall be placed at the foot of the list of such bills on the order paper.

Fisheries-building fishways and clearing rivers, $20,000.
May I ask the minister' to explain the work done under this vote?

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext: This appropriation is for the purpose of removing obstructions to fish ascending rivers and streams to their spawning areas and building fishways in dams across such rivers and streams. Particularly in British Columbia, log jams are forming continually and frequently become so complete that the ascending salmon are unable to get past them. In addition to that, natural obstructions are sometimes encountered which prevent the salmon from reaching the excellent spawning areas higher up the stream. Experience has proven that the removal of these obstructions invariably results in substantial increases in the runs of fish. In British Columbia during last year an expenditure of $11,260 was made. The list of the places where this money was expended is rather long; does my hon. friend desire that list?	.

No. There is a very important matter in coneetion with this item to which I direct the attention of the minister and of the department. While the run
TMr. McQuarrie.]
of salmon in British Columbia is very important, there is a certain difficulty on the rivers running into Hudson bay. Power companies are 'being allowed to build dams and obstructions on these rivers without giving the fish an opportunity to pass up in the spawning season. This may be a provincial matter as far as the construction of the dams is concerned, yet the construction of these obstructions prevents the run of fish into Hudson bay. The minister and the department will find that a number of power dams arc being erected in that part of the country with no arrangement made to permit of the passage of the fish. This is important not only to the province, but to the Dominion as well.

I would like to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that on the White Mud river, at the town of Gladstone, Manitoba, the Canadian Pacific Railway constructed a dam in order to provide water for their tank. In this dam there is no adequate means for the passage of the fish. This matter has been brought to the attention of the department for at least fifteen or eighteen years, and nothing has been done. It is only on very rare occasions, when the water is extremely high, that the fish are able to get over the dam. In ordinary years, when the ice goes out with comparatively low water, the fish come up to the bottom of the dam and remain there; they cannot get up the stream, where they desire to go. I draw this matter to the attention of the minister in the hope he will endeavour to have something done. There are many settlers above the dam who desire to obtain these fish in the spring, but on account of the dam they are unable to do so. I hope the minister and his department will look into the matter and see if something cannot be done to permit the fish to get up the stream in spring as they desire to do.

We have had one fishway built at that place but the technical officers advise that this is a very difficult situation to deal with. However, we propose this summer to send an engineer to look over the situation and advise us as to the possibility of coping with it. As far as my hon. friend from Kingston is concerned I may say that when a dam is built on a river the company is obliged to build a fishway according to the regulations established by the department.

But still these dams are being built with no arrangement of this kind. This is very important, because the spawning grounds of the fish are destroyed

and the settlers will suffer later. There are no fishways in these new dams which are being built for power purposes in that part of the country.
Has my hon. friend an-y particular river in mind?
I cannot give them all, but I can mention one, the Matagami river.

The law gives us power to impose upon the companies the obligation to build fishways in all their dams according to plans and specifications aproved by the department. Of course, it may be that the river to which my hon. friend is referring is in a province which administers its own fisheries.
While that may be true and the site of this dam may be within a provincial jurisdiction, yet the effect is on Hudson bay, so the matter becomes federal also.
I see the point.

I want to add to what has been said with reference to these dams. As far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned the construction of fishways is entirely overlooked, and some of our best rivers are destroyed because there is no fishway in the dam and consequently not a single fish can get up to the spawning grounds. This not only deprives outsiders of their sport but also deprives the people living along those rivers of an opportunity of employment and of the means of earning very considerable sums of money during the fishing season. There is one river in particular, a very excellent salmon river, which has been absolutely destroyed because of a dam built across the river without a fishway. That applies to a great many of our rivers, but when these matters are brought to the attention of either the federal department or the provincial department we are told that they will look into it, and that is .the end.' I protest against these dams being built across the rivers with no proper provision to permit the salmon to pass up to their spawning grounds.

I am very much surprised at the criticism of my hon. friend from Halifax, because I am informed by the director of fisheries that we are paying very close attention to this work in the maritime provinces and particularly in Nova Scotia. I am told that a certain number of these fishways would be of no effect at all in view of a change which has taken place in the con-

ditions obtaining on several of the rivers, but in order to be in a position to inquire I would like my hon. friend to give me the name of the river to which he has just referred.

I was referring to the East river, Sheet Harbour. I may say that I would be delighted to spend two or three days with the minister if he would care to come down to that province. I would take care of him and put him up and show him the .conditions which prevail, so that he could verify what I have been saying.

May I ask the minister if any further work is contemplated in clearing out Hell's Gate on the Fraser river, above New Westminster? The minister is perhaps aware that in 1913 the river was completely filled by a mountain slide caused by the operations of the Canadian Northern railway. Since 1913 there has not been a large run of sockeye salmon. Previous to that time in a big year, which occurred every fourth year, we had packs of sockeye salmon which ran up as high as a million cases. A case of sockeye salmon is worth about $16, and perhaps more. Since that time the highest pack that we have had on the Fraser river has been about 50,000 cases. I think the minister will realize the loss there is to the country by reason of the depletion of the run of sockeye on the Fraser river. It just happened that this slide took place during one of the big runs, just before the spawning season, and the salmon could not get through. It was understood that the rock had been removed from the bed of the river to allow the salmon in after years to proceed to the spawning ground, of which there are hundreds of thousands of acres above that point, but some of the people out there, and more particularly the Indians, are not satisfied that the river has been properly cleared. I believe that recently there has been some investigation made by engineers of the department, but I have not heard with what results. I do not know what is proposed to be done but it seems to me it is a point that should receive special consideration.

We have had working at this particular point, a board of engineers composed of engineers of the provincial and federal governments, but a report has not yet been made by that board. My hon. friend may rest assured that this matter has not been forgotten, and is being looked into. We realize the importance of it.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
When did the engineers start work?
About a year ago.

The reply that these reports are indefinitely delayed is not good enough. When I was complaining about the depletion of the sockeye run on the Fraser river I was told that the biological board Was making investigations. I asked when we might expect a report from that board and I was told possibly in ten years or so. This means a big loss to the country, and it seems to me that the engineers have had sufficient time to make a report. If the river has not been cleared it should be cleared out immediately.

I am informed, Mr. Chairman, that it is very important that we reach a proper decision. If a mistake is made, according to the information giveD to me by the technical officers of the department, it would mean the ruination of the whole fishing industry in that section. We are taking every precaution to make a complete study so that proper recommendations may be made.

I would like the minister to explain that because, as I understand it, it is just a question of taking out rock which fell into the bed of the river. What other question is involved there? How can that industry be seriously damaged when it has been almost completely wiped out already?

It may be very easy to say that it is only a matter of taking out a certain amount of rock, but I am told by the director of fisheries that if we take out a certain amount of rock at certain places it may change the direction of the river. At the present time a certain number of fish are going up that river, but if rock is taken out at certain points it will create such a current that the fish will be unable to pass through it.
You could not change the direction of the river at that point by anything short of an earthquake. If the minister had seen the river I think he would agree with me.

The currents would be
changed.

I would like to
mention the Indian river in Nova Scotia. This river gave up to flies over 200 salmon the last year it was fished, but because of the dam, not a fikh is to be had in it to-day.
I will send my hon. friend a complete statement regarding the two rivers he has just mentioned.

A large development is being carried on in the Mersey river in Queens county, where a number of dams are being constructed. This is a valuable river and I would ask that special attention be given to it.

Fisheries-to assist in the conservation and development of deep-sea fisheries and the demand for fish, $130,000.

To assist in the conservation of fisheries, and the demand for fish from deep sea waters, I would like to call the attention of the minister to something needed for the benefit of the fishermen in my constituency. At Cape Bauld considerable difficulty has been experienced for some years in protecting the fishing boats owing to lack of shelter facilities. The government built a pierhead about 100 feet long, but it is not long enough to give the protection required. There should be an extension of at least 100 feet to this pierhead in order that protection would be afforded the small fishing boats during rough weather. Considerable destruction has taken place there, both to boats and motors, and the fishermen feel that more business would be transacted and they would have a better opportunity of carrying on deep-sea fishing if this pierhead was extended. I think this could be done with an expenditure of about 810,000 or $12,000. I have previously called the attention of the department to this pier, and I would again suggest that this work be carried out. I realize that it would have to be done in co-operation with the Department of Public Works, and I would also direct the attention of the Minister of Public Works to this point. It is something that is really required. About 875,000 worth of lobsters alone go over this wharf every year, and a considerable quantity of potatoes are shipped -from twelve to fifteen thousand barrels. This expenditure should be made there in order to assist the farmers and the fishermen, and I ask the minister to consider this and see if something cannot foe done to relieve the situation there.

I am sure I will have the
support of every justice-loving member in this house in the matter I propose to bring up, and especially those from the maritime provinces, and more particularly from the

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
province of Nova Scotia. If the members will look at the foot of this page, they will see these words:
Authorized by statute - fishing bounty,

We have not come to that
item yet.

I am going to speak on it
under item 241, because we are not allowed to speak on a vote authorized by statute and it concerns the same matter. My hon. friends will, I am sure, be surprised to be told that, inadvertently no doubt, the province of Nova Scotia has been robbing the province of British Columbia of the sum of $80,000 annually for the last forty-six years. This is no phantasy; it is founded on law.
Is that why the British Columbia members want Hell's Gate opened?

You cannot give Hell's Gate
away, but you can give this away unless some action is taken now. The act is now chapter 74 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, and it is called the Deep Sea Fisheries Act. It was passed in 1882, that is forty-six years ago. What did the act do? It provided that an annual grant-I wish the committee to note that word-not a bounty, a grant, of $160,000 a year foe paid. Where was that grant obtained? By looking at section 2 we find that it is to be taken out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. Mark that, Mr. Chairman. There was not some earmarked fund set aside, but the money was to be taken out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. What was to be done with it? I again quote section 2. It was to be used-[DOT]
To aid in the development of the sea fisheries of Canada, and the encouragement of the building and fitting out of improved fishing vessels, and the improvement of the condition of the fishermen.
That is the fishermen of Canada. The act under section 7 took power to make regulations, as follows:
The governor in council may, from time to time, make such regulations as he deems necessary or expedient respecting the payment of the said grant and the manner in which applications for the same or any portion thereof shall be made.
And so on. It is just the regular phraseology that allows the minister to make regulations for the carrying out of the act. But it is an axiom of law-and I do not need to repeat it here-that parliament can give power to a minister to make regulations under an act, but those regulations must always be merely in an administrative capacity for
carrying out the act. They are confined entirely to the administration of what is in the act. It is absolutely ultra vires and impossible for parliament to confer, and it never does confer by an act of that kind, legislative powers on a minister; that is to say, he cannot under those regulations go out and make legislation or change the legislation concerning which he is authorized to make regulations. Just as recently as yesterday the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mc-Quarrie) quoted a reference to the supreme . court the other day of a matter in connection with British Columbia fisheries, and a great deal of the argument turned on that point. The judge who gave his decision alluded particularly to the fact that the Fisheries Act under a similar section gave the minister power to make regulations but not power to legislate.
But what the minister did in this case under the regulations was practically the same as if he had madte a new act. He might as well have said that this money should be given for the production of cabbages or sheep or something of that kind because, by means of regulation, he changed the whole spirit and intent of the act. I am not speaking about the present minister, of course, because this thing has been going on for forty-six years. By provisions made under the regulations the act was confined practically entirely to the maritime provinces and particularly Nova Scotia. They dared not do this in so many words because that would have been too raw, but they introduced, in connection with the application, language which practically confined the act to Nova Scotia. I notice they forbade applications to be made for this so-called bounty-it is not a bounty; it is a grant-by anyone engaged in fishing for salmon. One would suppose that fishing for salmon would come under the category of deep sea fisheries. I also find that they made provisions whereby people who went lobster fishing in Nova Scotia were qualified as 'being engaged in deep sea fisheries, although I do not think they go out so far to sea to trap lobsters as they do on the coast of British Columbia where we have trollers that go out thirty or forty miles to sea to catch salmon. That was the way in which the thing was worked. In addition to the provision against salmon taking it did not even allow British Columbia fishermen to qualify where they were engaged in cod or herring fishing. In other words they said indirectly what they could not and dared not say directly, namely, that British Columbia

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
was not to share in this grant which was announced to be entirely for the development of the deep sea fisheries of Canada.
A week or two ago I asked the government whether it was true that this money had been spent entirely on the Atlantic coast and the answer I got was yes. I also asked whether the government would take steps to see that the fishing industry on the Pacific coast got its fair share of the money and the answer I received was this:
As the bounty is based on the interest on Canada's share of the award made'under the fishery articles of the treaty of Washington, 1871, and as the said articles apply to the Atlantic coast only, the payment is restricted to that coast.
That is a very nice answer if you want to believe it, but you do not have to. In the first place it is a grant, not a bounty, and it is so specified in the act. I am not talking about what happened in 1871; I am talking about the act which was passed in 1882. When I am told that it is based on something that happened in 1871, I am reminded of an incident that happened in British Columbia. There was a case up in the supreme court and the lawyer who was arguing it happened to have been in the legislature at the time the particular act under discussion was passed. He insisted on telling the judge how he knew that the legislators when they passed the act intended such and so and meant such and so. He would say: "I was there and I know what the intention of the legislators was." Finally the judge got a chance to put in a word and he said: "Probably you were there and probably you know what the intentions were of the legislators, but unfortunately the government forgot to bind you up with the act. I have only the act before me and I must decide the law according to the act." That is the case here. We have nothing to do with the intention or what somebody thought or did not think in 1882. We have simply the act to bind us. I have a letter from an official of the department making a very valiant and desperate attempt to justify the action of the government in years past. He writes in part:
The fishing bounty-
I object to the word "bounty".
-grew out of the award of the Halifax commission which was made under the provisions of the Washington treaty of 1871.
And so on. I do not need to go into the details about the Washington treaty. I will say simply this. There were matters between the two governments and the two bodies of fishermen, American and Canadian. The
fMr. Neill.]
United States government agreed to pay the Canadian government a sum of money, which I think was $4,500,000, in consideration of our selling or giving them certain rights for their fishermen. In other words, Canada sold a little part of the rights of Canada, but my rights and your rights were sold just at the same time, as well as the rights of the fishermen of Nova Scotia, because they gave the Americans certain rights which were Canadian rights and they parted with a portion of those rights for $4,500,000. Very properly they took that money which belonged to the whole of Canada, just as the fish belonged to the whole of Canada, and placed it where? In a fund earmarked for this thing? No. It was placed in the consolidated revenue fund of Canada and we all know when money is placed there it is used entirely for the general good of Canada. The argument is used in the letter written by the department that this money was given to compensate the fishermen for their partial loss in sharing the privilege and therefore they were entitled to the interest derived from those sums. In the first place it was not given for that purpose; it was given to the whole people of Canada and not to one section of the people of Canada.
Let me give a very appropriate illustration. When the same conditions obtained in connection with the sealing award, they made a treaty between the United States and Canada, and the American government agreed to pay over a certain amount of money year by year from the proceeds of the sealing, and a considerable sum down in cash, but they paid that over to the government of Canada, and it went into the consolidated revenue fund. Parliament, it is' true, did take a very small sum and pay compensation to some sealers who had been immediately put out of business, but they held, and are holding to-day that that sum was paid for some rights belonging to Canada, and that it properly went into the consolidated revenue fund. However, that is more or less beside the point. The argument that I make is that whatever was thought or intended or wished at that time was not put into the statute. They say: It "grew" out of the treaty of 1871. Well, it took eleven years to grow, because the act was not passed till 1882, and all I am concerned with, and all we are concerned with here is, what did the act of 1882 say? For those eleven years that money lay in the consolidated revenue fund, and the interest was devoted to the common use of the finances of Canada, and there was no question of it being earmarked for anybody at all. They did not think of

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
that then. It was only in 1882, possibly because of some political exigency-I do not know-or perhaps because it was thought wise policy-at any rate they decided to vote $160,000 a year for the development of the sea fisheries of Canada, and that money has been spent, not for the benefit of the sea fisheries of Canada, but for the benefit of one small portion of the sea fisheries of Canada. Consequently we have been robbed, to put it in a blunt way, of our share of that money for that period.
It will be said that our fisheries were not in existence at that date, but that is not so. The salmon fishing of British Columbia had achieved considerable prominence even at that time. The trouble was that British Columbia was numerically inadequately represented in this house, and we suffered in consequence. When I was a child, being one of the younger members of the family, I suffered much from the theory largely believed in by my parents, and especially by my older brothers, that everything went to the older brother, and he had all the rights and privileges that were going. That feudal idea has disappeared now, and we in British Columbia, one of the younger members of the Dominion family as perhaps we are, feel that we are entitled to our fair share and to strict justice in this matter. I am asking, not for fair play, mot for equity, not for a compassionate arrangement, but just for that bare legal justice that we would accord even to an enemy alien in the darkest days of the war, for surely we would not refuse bare justice to anyone. We are not asking for a refund of our share of the $160,000 for forty-six years, which would be a considerable sum, or that we should get this amount exclusively for the next forty-six years. We are prepared to take a bigger view. We will make a grand gesture and say: Keep what you have got; we will not ask you how it was obtained, but we say that in the future we should share in the allocation of this money in proportion to the needs of the growing output of our fisheries and whatever is most urgent as between the two sides of the continent.
That the government themselves anticipated something of this kind will be found by referring to section 6 of the act which provides that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, whenever he deems it expedient to cause inquiries to be made in connection with any matter with respect to the grant or the payment thereof, shall direct that the inquiries be made.
There are many problems both on the Atlantic and the Pacific in connection with which this money could be far more wisely spent than in giving this trivial bounty of
one dollar to one man and six dollars to another. That does not do them any practical good, and it does not develop the sea fisheries of 'Canada. Take the British Columbia coast, for instance. There is a problem out there upon which a portion of this money could well be spent. The salmon going into the Fraser river go past our shores, but before they reach the Fraser they pass through Puget sound, where they are caught in enormous numbers in traps run by Americans who catch the big end of our Fraser river fish. If we did away with that, we would be in a position to make a treaty to-morrow with the United States. That is the stumbling block between us to-day. The United States are willing that we should have a close season and build up the Fraser river fish, but they want to take three-quarters of the catch in the future, as in the past. If we could develop this-some individual men have tried to do it, but they cannot afford to do it-if it was proved that these fish could be caught in our straits by gill nets-there are conditions of tide and current that govern fishing there-before they reach the United States traps, that would weigh heavily with the Americans, and we could make a treaty with the United States in six months.
There is another problem. That is in connection with the big pilchard industry that we have been developing in the last few years. The question will arise sooner or later whether these fish should not be caught out in the open sea instead of waiting until they get into the narrow inlets, where they are caught in such numbers that there is danger of scaring them away.
Then in connection with the trolling of salmon. No attempt has been made to trace the salmon, to find out where they come from, where they feed in the ocean, and in what way they approach our shores. That would be of great practical benefit to the fishing industry, and it would be worth fifty times a little hand out to a fisherman here and there. But I am not asking for any details. We are asking that in justice, and under the law as it stands in the act of 1882, a fair share of this money should be allocated to British Columbia or the Pacific coast in the future.

I have been very much interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, but surely he is not serious in the argument that he is attempting to put up for the Pacific coast, that British Columbia should participate in the bounty.

Not a bounty, a grant.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

It is a bounty. It was always understood that it was a bounty. It has been paid for the past fifty years. This sum of $160,000 represents the interest, as the hon. member well knows, on the award that was made at Halifax in 1878.

How should I know that?
Where do I find that?

The records show it. That was before there were practically any fisheries on the British Columbia coast.
Mr. M tie DONALD (Cape Breton): It was before British Columbia was a part of the Dominion.
British Columbia came into the Dominion long before 1882.

It was in 1878 that the award was made, and it never was paid. The government never decided to pay this bounty to the maritime provinces and Quebec until 1882, and consequently we Claim that there is interest of $160,000 for three years which is still unpaid and is still due to the fishermen of the maritime provinces. My hon. friend laughs, but there is no question about that. We have a well established claim to that money. The hon. gentleman well knows what the American government paid this money over to the Canadian government for. It was for certain privileges in regard to fisheries on the Atlantic coast, not on the Pacific coast. There were no fisheries on the Pacific coast at that time that amounted to anything, and the government did perfectly right in paying this bounty because the award was made for that puipose, and that purpose only. It has been paid for the past fifty years and it seems rather out of place now for a member from British Columbia to come forward, fifty years after this matter has been decided, to make a claim for the fishermen of British Columbia. I really cannot think that my hon. friend is serious in his demand, and I trust he will not press it, because it can only bring up a fruitless discussion. I am sure he is not going to take advantage of any little technicality there might- be in connection with the act and claim for British Columbia something that the province is certainly not entitled to. I am confident that we on the Atlantic coast would never think of making a claim for anything relating to the fisheries of the Pacific coast; and we expect of course the same treatment from our friends in British Columbia. I do not think this matter is worth discussing further, because it- was settled years and years ago and, as I say, the maritime provinces still claim that the interest for the three years

from 1878 to 1881 is due to us, amounting to-day to over half a million dollars. I hope the government will decide that that sum shall be distributed among the fishermen of the maritime provinces.
Carried.

Oh, no. I want an expression of opinion from the minister, but first of all I want to point out the absolute fallacy of my hon. friend's argument. He says: Everybody knows about this, it has been understood for fifty years. But when did age ever lend dignity to a wrong? If his argument is sound, see the extraordinary situation with which we are faced. If he has no better argument than to say I am striving for a technicality, then I submit my claim is proved, and I stand or fall by the act of 1882. Somebody says that British Columbia was not a member of the confederation at that time.
This award was made in 1878.

But I am talking of the act of 1882 which started this grant to our friend, and which now, not unnaturally, he wishes to retain when someone proposes to take it away from him. If I am not mistaken, British Columbia went into the union in 1871, but I am not quite sure.
Yes.

But I am sure it was in the union a long time 'before 1882, I am sure we had fisheries then, and I am sure we are entitled to a share of this money. If the minister is not prepared to make a statement I will ask the Miniscter of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), not for a legal opinion, for I know he will wriggle out of it-I do not need a legal opinion; I have consulted some of the best legal minds in Canada on this subject, and they say that legally I am absolutely right-but, if the Minister of Marine and Fisheries cannot see. his way to make a statement, (then I ask the Minister of Justice to say if he will issue a fiat to enable us to test this matter in the Exchequer Court of Canada, and so ascertain whether we are relying on a technicality or not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 242-
No, Mr. Chairman, you are not going to proceed until I get an answer from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am sorry, but I have just come in and do not know what my hon. friend is talking about.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
His colleague sitting beside him is fully acquainted with the matter and can easily fell him.

I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that I am not in a position to satisfy the request made by my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I am inclined to think that the practice which has been followed for the past fifty years has resulted in a certain interpretation of the statute regulating this matter. It as true that the statute does not state specifically that the money is to 'be distributed solely among the fishermen of the maritime provinces, but the interptetation placed upon this law by all governments since that time lead's me to believe that the real intention of the law-the spirit-has been understood as giving this privilege or advantage to the fishermen of the maritime provinces. In fact, the whole thing arose out of a difficulty at the time, which interested only the maritime provinces. As has been Stated, the treaty of Washington gave certain advantages to the fishermen of the United States, and certain reciprocal advantages were given to Canadian fishermen, but at the time it was thought that 'the balance of these advantages rested with the Americans. A joint board was appointed to investigate the matter, and it decided that the Canadian fishermen of the Atlantic coast-they were the only ones concerned in the negotiations-were to a certain extent prejudiced by the treaty, and the United States government paid four million dollars to the Dominion government by way of compensation. This money was paid in 1878. Since that time we have been paying the interest to the fishermen of the Atlantic coast, Reading the statute, not according to the strict letter but according to the spirit as interpreted by successive governments since that date, and taking into account the circumstances which gave rise to the legislation, I think it is fair to assume that the fishermen of the Atlantic coast are the people whom it was sought to compensate; and if the award was made for that purpose, it is only fair that those fishermen should be given the full advantage of the interest from that fund. I quite understand that from the purely legal point of view my hon. friend would be capable of making an argument-

Hear, hear.
Mr. 'SHORT: But only an argument.

-but I should not like him to entertain the idea that in the application of our laws and regulations we forget their spirit and the circumstances existing at the
time any case was dealt with. Those who suffered as a result of this treaty are, m my opinion, the people who should receive the compensation; that is only a matter of justice.
Will the minister give 'the committee some information as to how this bounty is distributed?

We distribute about $160,000 annually. One dollar is paid for each boat of a certain length which is used by the fishermen. Each fisherman must catch a certain quantity of fish to entitle him to the bounty.
What is done to conserve our deep sea fisheries?
Perhaps the member for AVet-askiwin (Mr. Irvine) will allow me to finish this subject?
Certainly.

I have this one word further to say in connection with the matter. If that was the spirit of the legislation when it was passed in 1882 the legislators must indeed have been chock full of spirit, or why did they not say so? Why was it not so expressed in the act? I cannot conceive of a body of legislators, passing an act like that, stating something entirely different from their supposed intention. As to the suggestion that because this thing has been going on so long it had better go on a little longer, I would remind the house of a recent example where this suggestion was not fallowed. I refer to Quebec's claim on Labrador, a claim that had been made for the last sixty years, but the Privy Council did not say: Well, having gone on so long the claim is valid. No, on the contrary, they said they would interpret the claim according to law. That is what I am asking the minister to do in this case, to adhere to the strict letter of the law. I may also say that in my view the suggestions I have made for the spending of this money would do far more good to our deep sea fishermen than giving a dollar to one man here and a dollar to another man there. That is not doing any good either to Nova Scotia or to any other part of the country. I want to ask the minister one more question. In view of the powers given him under section 6 of the act, would he be inclined to cause an inquiry to be made into the matter? That at least would give us some useful information.

At pages 66 and 67 of the fisheries commission's report, it is recom-

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
mended that the law be amended to meet the situation and obviate criticism. The idea is particularly to meet the objection of my hon. friend.

That is another proof that
my contention is correct.

How much does the minister propose to spend of this amount? This vote has been in the estimates each year, but last year only a small portion of it was spent- some $5,800. Out of this item an amount might very well be spent to create a demand for deep sea fish by means of advertising throughout the country. The money could not be spent in any better way. For two years the department spent $10,000 annually in conjunction with the dealers in the industry and a largely increased demand for fish was the result. The government should take out of this vote a sufficient sum-not a trifling amount like $10,000-to advertise deep sea fish throughout the length and breadth of the country. I understand that last year a small amount was used to put on a few collecting 'boats for the purpose of gathering up the fish in outlying districts and making it accessible to the market. How has that worked out? Was it satisfactory, and if so, is it the intention of the department to put more boats on this year so as to find a market for fish from the outlying districts?

Out of this vote we certainly could provide for some measure of advertising. Last year we contributed $10,000 to an organization and this has proved satisfactory. We can increase that contribution and this vote would cover the expenditure. Most of the money spent under the vote, which is relatively new, is intended to assist the marketing of fish.

Only $5,800 was spent last
year.

The vote has been increased materially in the last few years. We are using the money to help the marketing of fish as well as to -collect fish caught in small places where there are n-o facilities for transportation. That fish is brought to the more important centres where it can be marketed more readily.
Is it the intention to increase that this year?
Yes; we propose to extend that service.

I understand that not a
dollar was spent last year in advertising.
It was the year before.

Is this vote intended to
conserve deep sea fish or deep sea fisheries? It is not clear.
Deep sea fisheries.
What does that mean?

We encourage the fishermen and try to develop markets. Where fish can be marketed fresh, the fishermen make much better returns; hence it is desirable to extend the areas that can be served by fresh fish marketing. To this end an experiment was made in fish -collection along a portion of the coast of Guysborough, from Pickerton to Canso. Two boats were employed for the work early in July, and the service was continued until the end of the year. Towards the end of October a third boat had to be employed for a time to keep up the work. Each boat made three return trips per week, giving the coast a collection service every second day. This is more particularly contemplated to help those fishermen who are operating in small ports or on certain sections of the -coast where there are no facilities for the transportation of fish. We are assisting them in bringing their fish to the more important markets where it can be disposed of.
Were those boats equipped with cold storage?
No.

What was the total value
of the fishing industry in the maritimes last year?
In the vicinity of $20,000,000.

Item agreed to.
Fish culture, $442,000.

Has this to do with deep
sea fishing?
No.

In Scotland the idea was
prevalent among the fishermen that the trawlers destroyed the fishing beds as well as the fish. Has the minister taken cognizance of that situation? I believe that trawlers are active on the coast just now.

I should like some information regarding a matter I brought up last session; I refer to the depletion of streams and rivers of British Columbia, particularly the Chilliwack river. It was intimated that the department had already taken action in regard to stocking that river with steelheads. What progress has been made in the restocking of these streams with game fish?

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
The director of fisheries informs me that he is not in a position to give details, but generally speaking the work is followed up.

Will the minister tell us if any new work 'has been undertaken in regard to fish culture? I think this is the most important work of his department, and I would like to know if he has done anything new.

An appropriation was made in 1927-28 for building five hatcheries, but it was not found possible to complete the survey work required in selecting sites in time to have these hatcheries built. In addition, the Windsor hatchery is to be replaced1 and new hatcheries are to be built, one on the Lesser Slave lake, having to do with white fish. Then there is a trout hatchery on Waterton lakes.
Are these new hatcheries?
Yes.
Not some of the five which were proposed last year?

The appropriation last year was not sufficient to complete the work on these five hatcheries, and in addition the survey work was not completed. Hatcheries will be also located in northern Saskatchewan, Antigonish, Yarmouth and Windsor, and we propose to spend $175,000 on this work.

Following that, a more important point is whether the department has dhanged its policy in regard to the deposit of fry and fingerlings. There is a further item in the estimates to provide for fish culture in connection with the biological board, and there has been a great deal of constructive criticism to the effect that the department should adopt different methods. Has any other method been adopted in regard to the deposit of fry and fingerlings?

I am informed that the department is studying the matter in conjunction with the biological board, but no definite change in procedure has been adbpted. I am also informed that in certain places one system is more profitable than another, but all the work is earned on in conjunction with the board1 according to what is best in view of the circumstances.

The trouble has been that the suggestions of the board never have been carried out. Let me point out that in the United States a different policy has been adopted. We are still continuing the
deposit of fry and fingerlings in regard to pisciculture, and these fry and fingerlings are being destroyed, causing great waste. The United1 States has adopted1 a method by which these fingerlings are taken by separate clubs and kept for several months before they swe finally deposited in the streams. I am only directing attention to that fact because this discussion is now open, and this is a subject which is worthy of a great deal of attention. Waste has occurred in the past in this regard, and I think Canada should get more in line with modem methods in the distribution of fingerlings and fry.

Following the remarks of my hon. friend for Kingston, from my own experience, I am convinced that there is no doubt that we are wasting our time and1 our money in putting out fry and even fingerlings up to three and four inches in length. I might tell the minister that for four years in succession I have deposited some millions of fry in a lake the conditions of which from the point of view of fish culture, judging from a report made by the minister's own officer, are ideal. However, I have not seen any result whatever. That corresponds with the experience of scores of others not only in Nova Scotia but practically all over Canada where that work has been carried on. As the last speaker said, this question has been very freely discussed in the United States, and it is the opinion in that country that to deposit fry and small fingerlings is simply to waste effort, time and money. If we are going to attain any results we must keep these fry in the hatcheries or in some other place close by until they reach sufficient maturity to be able to dtefend themselves against their natural enemies, of which there are many. In other words, it is useless to put trout and salmon fry into our streams and liberate them under a length of say six inches, or more in some cases. I think that has been amply demonstrated, and I hope something will be done to remedy the enormous loss which we are suffering every year through the continuance of a practice which has proven valueless.

I understand the minister
gave the committee assurance yesterday that he was changing his attitude regarding the decision on the cancellation of the Bible

Students Association's license, and for that reason I was wondering what this commission was for. Am I correctly informed that the minister has decided to reconsider his decision in respect to the cancellation of that license?

That is not exactly what
I said. This vote provides for the acquiring of the necessary information before changing the whole situation regarding broadcasting. We want to inquire in England, the United States, and Canada as to the best means for Canada to adopt in dealing with radio broadcasting. We want to have this information before coming to parliament with a bill nationalizing the system, or some such method. We want to get the benefit of the experience of others before doing this. I said that I would have no objection to this commission looking into this particular case to see if any real injustice had been done.
Do I understand the minister to say that he will see that that is done?
Oh, yes, I will.

Is this commission to be of
a departmental character?

Not necessarily. I have
not made up my mind as to whom I will appoint. The main object is to get information; we will try to appoint a commission which will be qualified to get the information we need.

The commission
will be entirely advisory; nothing administrative about it?
Oh, no, absolutely advisory.

I quite agree with the desire of the minister to have a commission for this purpose. This is a matter which affects everybody in this country, and a proper inquiry by a commission would be most helpful. I would suggest to the minister that this commission ought to be appointed differently from many of the commissions heretofore; it should be a non-partisan commission. The members should not be selected on political grounds, but for their qualifications to give this question serious study. This is a question in which Conservatives are just as much interested as Liberals. This is not an inquiry into a partisan matter, and I hope the minister will not follow the plan which has been followed with some other commissions in appointing a man purely for political reasons.

I notice a difference of

I want to ask the Minister [DOT] of Agriculture what arrangement he has made for the settlement of the claim that Mr. Pendrell Smith of Kamloops has against the department? I have had this claim up with the minister now for more than two years.
It is for a certain salary for certain work done 'by a member of his department, which salary the minister refuses to pay. I should like to have the thing finally and flatly settled.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
My recollection is that Mr. Smith was holding down two jobs, and that is contrary to the usual practice in government circles. So he was deprived of one salary, which was a very modest one and the smaller of the two, in connection with car inspection, the maximum salary for which would be about $200 a year at that point. That is just my recollection of the circumstances. The claim of Mr. Smith was that some back pay had been retained. After going into the matter very carefully we considered that his claim was not well founded.
I told my hon. friend a few days ago that I would have it reviewed, but in the rush of the last few days of the session I have not yet succeeded in doing that.

The minister says that
the action taken is on account of his holding two positions. I should like to know on what grounds he bases the statement that he cannot pay a man for two positions in the same department. Is it contrary to the provisions of the Civil Service Act?

I understand that
is contrary to the provisions of the Civil Service Act. At all events the Civil Service Commission declines to make two appointments go to the one man.

I want to read to the minister section 17 of the Civil Service Act which applies to the matter. Section 17 reads:
In the absence of special authority of parliament no payment additional to the salary authorized by law shall be made to any deputy head, officer, clerk or employee permanently employed _ in the civil service in respect of any service rendered by him, whether in the discharge of his ordinary duties of office or of any other duties which may be imposed upon him, or which he may undertake or volunteer to discharge or otherwise perform.
2. Nothing in this section is intended to prohibit the payment to any officer, clerk or
Supply-Agriculture

employee of a separate annual salary from each of two or more departments or distinct branches of the civil service in respect of separate duties performed for each of such departments or branches respectively, if one of such salaries is not sufficient to compensate him for his whole time, and if the aggregate salaries do not, in the opinion of the deputy head, concurred in by the commission, exceed reasonable compensation for the discharge of all the duties so performed.
I want to tell the minister that the total salary earned by this gentleman for the two positions was about $825 per annum. Does he consider that is sufficient salary for a man for a whole year? Both of these are seasonal occupations; neither of them extends throughout the year. Out of that amount of $825 per annum the minister is deducting $146 because the man is employed in two different branches of the same department. The officers of the department are absolutely certain of the fact that the services have been faithfully performed. They are anxious to pay the money and the heads of the department refuse to pay it. The duties do not conflict in any shape or form.

How many months would
he work?

I am not sure, but I think about five months in the whole year. The duties start in about August and they end in the beginning of the year when the fruit season is over. The stock car inspection work, I imagine, continues throughout the year. The salary which he should receive for this work but of which he is denied payment amounts to from $15 to $20 a month. He was appointed first as a stock car inspector, receiving an average of $15 to $20 a month. Afterwards the Civil Service Commission advertised for a junior fruit car inspector for the Kamloops district. This is a seasonal occupation lasting about five months. This gentleman, as I say, was at that time occupied as inspector of cars of live stock at a salary of $15 to $20 a month. When the position of junior fruit car inspector was advertised he sent in his application and he stated on it that he was temporarily, part-time employed as stock car inspector. The application was accepted with that statement on it, and he was appointed as fruit car inspector at a salary of $125 per month for the season, which I understand is about five months of the year. This information was before the department when the appointment was made. He carried on both of these duties for the five months and he was not advised until after the expiration of the five months that he would not be paid

the amount he was earning from time to time for the inspection of stock cars. That has been refused from that time till now. The gentleman, as a matter of fact, has been discharged by the department for some reason. I do not know what the reason is and I am not inquiring about it. It may be a very good reason for all I know. The point I am making is that when his appointment was made it was definitely stated to the commission and to the department that he was a part-time employee and they raised no objection to that at the time. They allowed him to go on for five months making these inspections of stock cars and they now refuse to pay him something like $146, which he has earned. They also neglected to notify him that he would not be paid for the inspection of the stock cars. Had they so advised him, he would have refused to inspect them. The department is absolutely satisfied in regard to the inspection of the cars. The work was well done and yet they r.efused to pay him. Under the circumstances the department surely cannot refuse to pay this gentleman. The minister quotes the Civil Service Act as his authority for refusing to pay this sum, but my interpretation is that there is nothing in the section to prevent the payment.

Before the minister replies,
may I point this out generally for hon. gentlemen who are supporters of the government as well as for our opponents politically, including my hon. friend who has quoted the Civil Service Act in support of his argument? That has no application
to this case because the man has already lost his position. He has lost it for some work in regard to an election which the government says is objectionable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought he was lobbying
for an increase.
No, he is lobbying for money that he actually earned and which the officials of the department say they are absolutely willing to pay, and the man should be paid, but the minister refuses to pay him.

It is some time
since I reviewed the case, therefore the details are not so clear to me as I would like to have

them in order to maike a specific statement, but I remember this much, that the accountant of the department claimed that this claim could not be paid. It is not an alleged claim.
I cannot allow the minister to get away with that. There is another point. With all due respect to the minister and all due deference to his opinion, I think it is about time that a claim of that kind was settled. After having followed this thing up in two different sessions, and getting this information from the department, if I had any reason to believe that the claim was not founded on justice I would not bring it up on the floor of the house; that is a certainty. The man did the work, and that is recognized by the officials of the department.

We will look into
it.

They would have had to
pay somebody else if he had not done the work, and they did not advise him that he would not be paid until after he had done the work. He has only been paid $825 for the whole year, and then you deduct $146 for this stock car inspection. It does not seem fair to me, and the minister knows it does not seem fair to him.
We have no desire to hold anything back.

I agree that you do not
desire to do it, but just the same you have done it and you are doing it now.

No, we have not
done it.

This is rather a large
item and I notice an increase of $175,000. I would ask the minister if out of this $175,000, he is providing grants for class B fairs.
No, Mr. Chairman
I should like to ask the minister why he is dropping the grants for class B fairs.

The story is somewhat a long one, and it is pretty near lunch time, but I will do the best I can. The first year after I had the honour to have charge of this department I looked into the matter of grants to all the fairs quite thoroughly and I tabled a return this year dealing exhaustively with grants both for winter and summer fairs all over Canada.
Briefly, before the war there was a federal grant of $50,000 to a perambulating Dominion fair, which was held in practically every province. During the war that grant was stopped, and in lieu of it certain grants were given to the larger fairs throughout Canada, which were subsequently classified into class A and olass B fairs. This was done purely as a war measure because of the difficulty the fairs found in financing. During the war it was at one time thought of suspending all these exhibition grants in order that the federal government and the governments of the provinces might confine their attention more particularly to war purposes, but it was decided eventually to give grants to a number of the medium sized fairs and interprovincial fairs, running up to two or three hundred thousand dollars in the aggregate. That was done as a war measure and as a war measure only. In 1922 I gave notice to these fairs that the grant must be dropped off, but I promised that until their finances were in better shape we would continue to pay the grant for two or three years. That was done, but at the end of the two or three years, we extended the period, and in fact extended it on three different occasions. I do not wish to repeat the arguments which most of the members have made here to-day, because it would be superfluous. But I do say that it is very unfortunate that these grants are being discontinued to the B circuit fairs. They are doing a great work, and a work that is just as much national in its character as the Toronto fair.

I wrote to the
departments of agriculture in Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan to find out what they had done with respect to their respective fairs in anticipation of the federal grants being dropped. Everybody knew that this adjustment was going to take place, because they had been given warning, and in anticipation of our dropping these grants the provincial governments in some cases were raising theirs. That was not done in all cases, because some fairs had got into hard circumstances, trying to keep up with the Joneses, and they could not earn a larger grant from the provinces. I would point out to my hon. friend that Vegreville got S985.83 in 1918 from the provincial government, and in 1927 it received also from the provincial government 82,426 for its exhibition alone.

I should like to say
one word on this subject, which I think is rather important. As I understand the minister's contention, and I recognize the difficulty of his position, these grants are being withdrawn on two main grounds. The first is that they were given in the first place as a war measure, when conditions were not normal, and now ten years after the war these grants are being dropped. The second is that continuing these grants would make it almost impossible to draw the line between B class fairs, C, and so on all down the line, and would involve the minister and his department in a tremendous amount of obligation. I have had a little experience, as most of us have had, having been in the west for forty years or so; I have visited the different

kinds of fairs we have, and I know the work they are doing. We have in my constituency a number of small fairs, in addition to one B class fair in Red Deer. I also have been glad to attend the larger fairs in the larger centres whenever I had the opportunity, and I have been endeavouring to see to what extent the money has been spent to the best advantage, and' generally what value the country has been getting from the money expended under these grants.

You mean federal
grants?

Yes, to see where the
money was spent to the greatest advantage; not for providing amusement, but for actually improving the quality of our live stock and the standard of farming throughout the country. As I understand it, that is one of our greatest national works. From that point of view I do not think it is very difficult to differentiate between what we call B fairs and those further down the list. I suggest it would be well to set a certain standard to which those B fairs must attain or else lose the grant. My experience is that the smaller fairs are purely local in their character; they are attended by the farmers in the district, who bring in their stock for competition. But the B fairs are more than local, they draw their exhibits from all over the province, and sometimes from other provinces. In other words, as an object lesson in quality of stock they stand pre-eminently above the smaller and purely local fairs. In that respect they come more nearly to a parity with the large provincial fairs whose grants are being continued. From that point of view I believe it would be sound policy within reasonable limits-and no one can say that $33,000 in grants to the smaller fairs throughout a country like Canada is an unreasonable expenditure-to treat as permanent the grants to those fairs which are endeavouring to improve the! quality of our stock and our methods of farming.
Then there is another thing to be taken into consideration-and undoubtedly it was regarded at the outset-the financial position of these fairs and their opportunities of obtaining money from other sources. Those sources are very few, and the principal are of course the gate receipts. Those gate receipts are becoming more and more dependent on the side shows, the grandstand performances and other circus features, which, regarded from the proper point of view, are not educational agriculturally. The more nearly the fair approaches the proper type, the type

Supply-Agriculture-Exhibitions
intended as an educational factor, the type intended to give an object lesson to the whole country as to the class of farming carried on and the quality of stock raised, the more nearly it approaches the ideal. And it follows that the less stress laid on what I term the purely circus features, the side shows and so on, and the more on stock judging and the other important factors, the smaller, as a whole, will be the gate receipts. At Calgary and Edmonton we find the gate receipts running into the tens of thousands of dollars, paid for the most part by people not five per cent of whom ever go near the stock and farming exhibits. Those people attend to see the grandstand performances and to look at the side shows, the circus and the fireworks. But those two fairs are allotted grants which they do not require in anything like the same degree as the smaller shows, because the very nature of the extraneous attractions at the big fairs swell the gate receipts.
I recognize the difficulty confronting the minister, but in the interests of the Dominion he should do his utmost to build up the basic industry to the highest point possible by encouraging the production of better stock and the bringing together at these fairs of samples of that better stock from all over the province and from the other provinces as well. To this end I suggest that it would be sound policy to make permanent what was commenced purely as a war measure; and to do away with or lessen the difficulties of the smaller fairs I suggest he should stipulate the conditions under which grants will be made, thus giving all possible encouragement to those fairs to develop stock-judging competitions, which would be of great educational value to our agriculturists and stock men. This policy in my opinion would be preferable to the policy that is being pursued right now of putting a premium, so to speak, on the side show and circus features of these fairs to the disadvantage of the great basic industry of agriculture.

What would my
hon. friend do with such a case as that referred to by another hon. member, the Willow Bunch fair, which has grown up from infancy-would he let that class of fair in?

Instead of the $33,000,
I think $100,000 would be well spent in grants to fairs that live up to the proper conditions, that is, so conduct their operations as to educate the people in improving the quality of their stock and their methods of farming.
But would he permit such fairs to come in as B fairs?
Yes.

You would have
them by the score.
Well, I would welcome them if they lived up to all the conditions that I have stated, and I think the money would be better spent.

Another question.
Every time I have a conference with any agricultural association, particularly provincial, I am implored to cut out overlapping of activities. Well, the further we go with these grants the more we overlap the provincial grants. That is the one outstanding complaint from the provincial departments of agriculture, that our work is overlapping theirs. Now, if I take the advice of my hon. friend, good as it is, I would be overlapping more and more every year. And I want to assure my hon. friend that we could not stop at the point he indicates-the C fairs think they are as good as the B, and the result is that in a democratic country such as this, where you have to hearken to the electorate, there is no place to stop until you get to the bottom, the smallest and most humble exhibitions in the Dominion. That is my experience.

I realize the objection to overlapping. I realize, too, that if that objection was carried to its logical conclusion there would be no federal department of agriculture at all. But to my mind that overlapping could be better avoided by the minister saying:	We will take over as a
federal obligation those fairs that reach the proper standards, and the provinces can devote their whole attention to the smaller fairs. In other words, subdivide the territory. Then each authority could do better work, and there would be no overlapping.

In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) is quite sound in his views. The weak spot of the ministers' policy appears to be that by encouraging Toronto and the other large exhibitions he is centralizing the whole system. If you consider the exhibits at, say, the Toronto exhibition, you will find that eventually, if this policy is continued, the small! breeder will be forced out, because he cannot compete with any hope of success against the millionaire who to-day takes up stock-breeding as a hobby. The idea of making grants to the large centres rather than

to the small is in my opinion not in the interests of agriculture. The hen. minister spoke wisely when he stated that if he continued giving to one fair after another he would he accused of overlapping; but I think he might very well overcome that objection by handing his grants to the provincial ministers of agriculture, with the stipulation that they must be distributed among a certain class of fairs. In that way he could not be accused of overlapping provincial work. I will give him the experience of Renfrew. He has in that county one fair which is decidedly class B and which is perhaps, next to Toronto, one of the best and most representative fairs in the province of Ontario. It is in the town of Renfrev^. That fair never received a grant from this government as a class B fair. When I see towns in the west, one-third the size of Renfrew, with fairs whose prize lists do not compare at all with the prizes given at Renfrew, but who nevertheless receive grants, I can say only this, that the policy that has been, pursued has been indeed unfair. There has been no overlapping so far as Renfrew is concerned. In the town of Arnprior-
Does the hon. member consider that it is the towns cr the agricultural districts that are entitled to such a system?
I am speaking now of exhibits, the total value of exhibits.
Agricultural or industrial?

This is related to live stock. It is an agricultural fair, but this particular branch has reference to live stock exhibits. What I have said with regard to Renfrew applies with almost, equal force to the town of Arnprior. Neither of these fairs ever received any consideration from this minister, or from any other minister for that matter. After all, it is the small breeder, the man who takes an interest in the breeding of 3toek in the small centres on different farms, to whom we must look in the long-run, and not to the millionaire who is interested in stock breeding as a hobby. If we wish to encourage the breeding of stock broadcast, then I say to the minister, hand over to the various departments of agriculture in the provinces a certain sum each year, that money to be distributed in conjunction with grants given provimciailly, and let the class be stipulated. If the minister continues as he has been doing in the past, we will make a demand

for Renfrew, and many demands will be made from this province for fairs which dpserve and have deserved grants which they have not received.
Is my hon. friend in favour of Renfrew receiving a federal grant?
Absolutely.
That proves what I say. If we continue these grants to B fairs every fair like that of Renfrew will want a grant.

I have advised you how you may overcome the difficulty. Give a substantial grant to each provincial department and let them distribute the money. If you do not feel equal to distributing it, leave it to those who know the situation and let them distribute the money.
That would be an unusuail Way.

I have a great
deal of sympathy with the minister in the position in which he finds himself. He is suffering to-day and has been for some time, as the result of an unwise economic policy adopted in the past, a policy which in my opinion cannot be justified on its merits. I refer to the policy of assisting certain fairs and withholding assistance from others. That is something that developed out of conditions over which probably no one had any considerable control. I agree with the minister that the condition should be remedied, but where I object, to the procedure of the minister is in the method he seeks to adopt by which to remedy the injustice that exists. I find myself in much greater accord with the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Fan-sher). That hon. member enunciates a principle which is absolutely sound throughout the country; that is, that it is not to those who need assistance the least that assistance should be given, but rather the centres which are doing genuine agricultural development work, and who stand most in need of assistance. There is and has been for many years in this country a tendency to encourage large places and large enterprises at the expense of smaller and growing communities, whether rural or urban. By this means a great deal of the wealth of Canada has been concentrated in cities and problems have arisen, from that concentration, in connection with industrial development. And we are now threatened with the same condition in relation to the development of agricultural fairs. It is abso-

Supply-Agriculture-Exhibitions
lutely wrong for us to give large sums of money by way of assistance to fairs which financially do not require any assistance at all, while at the same time we cut out the aid to smaller places which are functioning well in the interests of improved agriculture, particularly as regards stock and grain growing. The fairs which are receiving assistance under the head of class A fairs have not been enumerated, but we are told that the Toronto fair gets $5,000. Now, everyone knows that the Toronto fair has been earning profits, not at the rate ,of $5,000 a year but something like from $40,000 to even $200,000 a year for many years back. One or two years ago I put on record in this house the net earnings and profits of the Toronto national fair. Not long ago I saw the figures brought up to date, showing that the profits have increased largely in the past two years. They do not need that $5,000 in the slightest degree. The royal fair at Toronto is probably in a different position, but even here we see the result of a wrong system-the concentration in one city of $60,000 per annum for the promotion of agricultural interests of the Dominion. At the same time we are cutting out the smaller sum of $33,000 spread throughout the Dominion. The statement has been made by the Minister of Agriculture to-day-and it is right-that $50,000 was spent before the war in a perambulating fair. Possibly that was entirely justified. If I remember correctly, though, it was the intention that after the perambulating fair had visited every province in Canada that branch of endeavour should not be continued.
I don't think it.

That is my
memory; I do not argue the point however. I accept the word of the minister.

I understand from
my deputy that you are right.

Yes; generally
I can trust my memory to a certain extent at least. The province of Prince Edward Island was not able to take advantage of that grant by reason of local conditions. Now, what situation do we find to-day? We are told that the $33,000 must be cut down because there is no stopping place. I agree with the minister that there would be no limitation unless restrictions and1 regulations were framed in regard to the number of these fairs. But in connection with the larger fairs, what is the situation? Something like $275,000 is being spent now in the encouragement of the larger fairs. The hon. member for Red
Deer a moment ago observed-I cannot recall his exacts words, but I will give his meaning -that these larger fairs consist largely of industrial exhibits, sideshows, entertainments, stampedes and other features perhaps worse than any of these I mention, while the agricultural element constituted the minor feature. Anyone watching people going into these large fairs will see them make at once for the sideshows, the grandstand, the horse races and that class of entertainment. But if he visits the barns, as I invariably do when I go to a fair, he finds within a short distance of them the absence of any crowd. There is no competition there; no one is jostling anybody off the sidewalk. The crowds do not concentrate around the barns. Yet we find that to-day these fairs, where this condition prevails, are getting the sum of $275,000 as against $50,000 voted once in each province in connection with a perambulating fair. If the argument is sound that grants to the class B fairs should be discontinued because the assistance was given as a war measure, the argument is five times as forcible in relation to these other fairs. I think it would be a wise move either to abolish the grants altogether or to continue them on the basis of a perambulating grant to the provinces, to be repeated every nine years, at approximately the rate paid before the war. The minister has a serious objection against the smaller fairs increasing in number so as to become an embarrassment to the Dominion treasury, yet I find that to-day he is inviting another city to stage a fair and apply for this grant. The minister says he understands Winnipeg proposes to come into this class later on, and that if she does she will be entitled to the larger grant. I suggest that in view of the very important work being done by the smaller fairs, this grant should be continued. It is very small, hardly worth fighting over, but these fairs are doing good work and they should continue to receive this assistance.
Before I sit down perhaps I should draw a contrast between the larger and the smaller fairs. In the district which I have the honour to represent, a district 180 miles wide by 500 miles from north to south, there is an area of about 100 miles by 60 miles which is well settled agriculturally. In that district there is one class B fair to which stock are brought from all over that district. Farmers and their families and associates can come to that fair on any one of the three days for which it lasts. It costs a man living fifty or sixty miles away very little to put himself and his family into his car, drive to town, pay the admission for himself and his

Supply-Agriculture-Exhibitions
family and have a full day's enjoyment and entertainment. I regret that even small fairs seem to think they must have entertainment, but at any rate a man visiting that fair has a long day's entertainment and education in viewing the stock and exhibits. Then he goes to his car and drives home with his family, arriving there in plenty of time to take up his work the next day.
Contrast that with the fairs in the large cities. If a man desires to go to the fair he finds it very difficult to take anyone but himself; it is expensive both in time and in money as well as inconvenient for himself and his family to be away from home for so long. The smaller fair overcomes that difficulty entirely. The argument is made that the larger fairs are interprovincial, and that their exhibits are received from the different provinces. That is so, but the smaller fairs obtain exhibits from provinces just as far distant. Many exhibitors at the smaller fairs make the statement that they are able to do much more business in the selling of live stock than is the case at the larger fairs, because the farmers from the surrounding districts come to the small fairs and devote their time to a study of the live stock, and they are much more at liberty to discuss business and consider the purchase of live stock as foundation stock than are the farmers who attend the large fairs.
I think it is important that we continue for some time this assistance to these fairs. I do not think the department can go on indefinitely increasing the grants to any fairs whitih may apply for them; personally I should like to see the grants cut down, because I think this is a provincial responsibility. However, so long as the large fairs receive something like $275,000 a year I object to the smaller fairs being cut out of the $33,000 they now receive. Two years ago these grants were reduced about forty per cent on the ground of economy and because the money could be used to greater advantage elsewhere, and very little objection was made. If the grants to the larger fairs were reduced in the same way and abolished next year I think it would be all right, because then the provinces would have to attend to this matter. No doubt there is considerable overlapping, and I agree with the minister that it is a bad policy for the government to be spending money on the same objects for which the provincial governments are spending money, but I do not think this is the best way to stop the practice. Something should be done, and I should be glad to see a definite policy of reduction put into effect.

I think if we are
to abide by the understanding which was

reached we should either pass this vote, and apparently we are not ready for that yet, or ask that the committee rise and report progress, which I now do.
